output:
# My grooming van nearly caught fire. Looking tidy didn’t make it safe.

Last Wednesday, October 28, at about 2:15 in the afternoon, I was standing in a client’s driveway in Bedford, drying a damp Bernese mountain dog called Moose, when I smelled hot plastic.

My first thought was the dryer motor.

It was running on high. Moose has enough coat for several dogs. Nothing about that part of the afternoon felt unusual.

Then I saw smoke coming out from under the bench seat where the batteries are.

I switched off the battery switch, got Moose out through the side door and used the extinguisher a bit. I honestly don’t know whether I needed to use it, but I wasn’t going to stand there and wait to find out.

Moose was still damp and absolutely delighted to be outside. He was the only one having a good time.

Everyone is fine. That is the important bit, and I keep coming back to it.

But the positive cable connection was blackened, the cable jacket had melted back about three centimetres, and my van is now off the road for at least three weeks.

My whole income is in that van.

I’m writing this partly because I need to get it out of my head, but mostly because other groomers read this blog. My friend Tasha is about to pay a deposit on a conversion with the same builder. I want her—and anyone else buying or working out of a grooming van—to know what happened and what to ask before handing over money.

**I’m not an electrician. Please don’t use this post as instructions for rewiring your van.** What follows is what happened to me, what the electrician found, and the things I wish I’d known to ask.

## What was in my van

My conversion was built by Darren at Coastline Van Fitouts in spring 2025.

The electrical setup included:

- A 3,000-watt inverter.
- Two 200Ah lithium batteries in a 12-volt system.
- A 4 AWG cable supplying the inverter from the batteries.
- A 300-amp ANL fuse.

I trusted the build because it looked tidy. Cables tucked away, connections covered, everything looking like somebody had thought it through.

I didn’t know how to tell whether the cable was properly sized. I didn’t know what a good high-current crimp looked like underneath heat-shrink. I wasn’t asking where the fuse was in relation to the battery.

I knew how to groom dogs. I thought I was paying someone else to know those things.

Since the incident, Priya from Sackville Marine Electric has inspected the installation. The cable size, the positive cable termination and the fuse location were all things she flagged.

Those are separate issues. Put together, they are a very unpleasant list.

## The numbers I didn’t understand before

The inverter takes power from the batteries and turns it into power my equipment can use.

Here is the bit that finally made sense to me: a 12-volt battery system has to supply a lot of current to run a powerful appliance.

The basic calculation is:

**Watts ÷ volts = amps.**

My dryer draws roughly 1,800–2,000 watts. At exactly 12 volts, that works out to:

- 1,800 watts ÷ 12 volts = **150 amps**.
- 2,000 watts ÷ 12 volts = **about 167 amps**.

That is before allowing for the inverter’s losses. It doesn’t turn every watt from the batteries into a watt at the socket.

As an illustration, at 90% inverter efficiency, a 2,000-watt load would need about **185 amps at 12 volts**. The actual figure depends on the battery voltage and the inverter’s efficiency at that moment.

If the water heater is running as well, the total demand goes up. I don’t have a measured combined load from the incident, so I can’t honestly say exactly how many amps were flowing when the cable overheated.

The inverter’s full 3,000-watt output would mean **250 amps at 12 volts before losses**, or about **278 amps at 90% efficiency**.

So my original scribble of “150–250 amps” was a rough picture, not a measured reading or a reliable upper limit.

Either way, we’re talking about serious current.

Also, “3,000-watt inverter” describes its rated output, not what it draws constantly. The battery current depends on what is running. But the installation still needs to be designed around the inverter manufacturer’s requirements and the loads it is intended to support.

Having big batteries does not make an undersized cable safe. Battery capacity and cable capacity are different things. I know that now.

## What Priya found with the cable

The battery-to-inverter cable was **4 AWG**.

Priya told me that, for my 3,000-watt, 12-volt installation, it should have been **2/0 AWG**.

The sizing names are confusing if you’ve never dealt with them. The useful bit is that **2/0 is much bigger than 4 AWG**.

I’m deliberately saying “for my installation” here. I don’t want somebody reading this and ordering cable based only on a blog post.

The right size depends on more than the wattage printed on the inverter. Cable length, insulation rating, routing, temperature, bundling, acceptable voltage drop and the equipment manufacturer’s instructions all matter. The positive and negative sides of the circuit both need to be considered.

Priya’s assessment was that my main inverter cable was undersized.

That does not mean every cable marked 4 AWG is dangerous. It means a cable that is suitable for one job may be completely wrong for another.

I wish I had asked for the inverter’s installation requirements and the actual cable specification before the build was finished.

## The connection hidden under the heat-shrink

The positive lug was the other horrible discovery.

A lug is the metal fitting on the cable end that attaches to a terminal. On a connection carrying this much current, the way that lug is attached matters enormously.

Priya said mine appeared to have been crimped with something like pliers or a hammer, rather than the proper crimping equipment for that cable and lug.

Heat-shrink was covering it.

From the outside, I hadn’t seen anything that made me question it.

A poor connection can create resistance in one small area. With high current flowing, that resistance produces heat. The electrical relationship is current squared times resistance, which means a little extra resistance can become a big problem when the current is high.

I am not going to pretend I can reconstruct every second of what happened under that seat. I can say that the positive lug was blackened, the insulation had melted back, and Priya identified a poor termination as a serious problem.

This is also why “but there was a fuse” isn’t the reassurance I once thought it was.

A fuse is not a temperature sensor attached to every connection. A bad joint can overheat while the overall current remains below the level that makes the fuse open.

That was a particularly nasty thing to learn after the fact.

## The fuse was about 90 centimetres from the battery

My installation had a **300A ANL fuse**, mounted roughly **90 centimetres from the battery**.

Priya said it should have been much closer—around **18 centimetres** for the arrangement she was describing.

I’m not presenting 18 centimetres as a universal rule for every vehicle installation. Exact requirements and permitted exceptions depend on the applicable standard, equipment and how the cable is protected.

The reason for keeping battery overcurrent protection close to the source, though, is straightforward: **the cable between the battery and the fuse is not protected by that fuse against a short in that section.**

Moving the fuse farther away leaves a longer section exposed to that risk.

And fuse selection is more than choosing a number that looks big enough. It has to work with the cable, equipment and battery system.

Priya’s repair quote includes a **Class T fuse**. One relevant consideration with lithium batteries is whether a fuse can safely interrupt the very high fault current the battery system may be capable of supplying.

That doesn’t mean I’m declaring every ANL fuse unsuitable for every lithium installation. It means the fuse type, current rating and interrupting rating need to be checked for the actual system—not guessed.

I am very happy to leave that calculation to someone qualified.

## The pictures that really got to me

Priya put my damage photos beside thermal-camera images of her own van operating under a similar kind of load.

Hers barely got warm.

Mine had a blackened connection and melted insulation.

It wasn’t a laboratory comparison, and a thermal image alone doesn’t prove an installation is safe. But seeing the two beside each other made something click.

This wasn’t just “well, dryers use a lot of power, so cables get hot.”

There were specific problems to investigate. Heat and damage were not something I should accept as a normal part of running my equipment.

I keep thinking about how tidy everything looked before.

**Tidy is not the same as right.**

## What I wish I’d had in the back

There wasn’t a smoke detector in the grooming area.

There was only the one in the cab that came with the van. I had mentally filed that under “the van has a detector” without asking what it was intended to detect or whether it could give useful warning from the battery area.

That assumption needs fixing.

I’m getting advice on suitable smoke detection and placement for the conversion, including the battery area. Grooming vans have moisture, hair and products to account for, so this is another thing I want chosen properly rather than stuck wherever there’s room.

I also want my extinguisher checked after using it, and I want someone qualified to confirm that the type and location make sense.

What I did in a fright is not an emergency procedure for anyone else to copy. If you see smoke or fire, get people and animals out, stay out and call 911. Only isolate power if you can do it without putting yourself at risk. Don’t reach into a smoking battery compartment.

There is nothing under a bench seat worth getting trapped over.

## A power-off checklist for your own van

This is a **look-and-document checklist**, not a repair guide.

Switching off the inverter does not necessarily disconnect its battery supply. A battery switch may not isolate every circuit either. Shore power, solar charging and other supplies can complicate things.

If you don’t know how your system is isolated, don’t open electrical compartments to investigate. Ask an electrician to show you.

Even with switches off, treat battery terminals and nearby conductors as live. No tools, jewellery or hands near exposed connections. Don’t remove protective covers, peel back heat-shrink, tighten terminals or disconnect cables for this checklist.

### 1. Look for damage from a safe position

Without disturbing anything, can you see:

- Melted, browned, cracked or distorted insulation?
- Discoloured terminal covers?
- Soot or scorching?
- Cable rubbing against a sharp edge?
- Loose-looking mounting or unsupported cable runs?
- Water getting into an electrical area?

A lingering hot-plastic smell counts as a warning too.

If you find heat damage, stop using the affected system and get professional advice. Don’t turn it back on to see whether it happens again.

### 2. Photograph the labels you can safely see

Collect the inverter make and model, battery labels and any visible fuse markings.

Photograph cable markings only if they are readable without moving cables or reaching near terminals.

If something is hidden, write down “unknown.” That is useful information for an electrician. You do not need to uncover it yourself.

### 3. Find your paperwork

Do you have:

- An electrical diagram?
- The inverter and battery manuals?
- Cable sizes and run lengths?
- Fuse types and ratings?
- Installation or commissioning records?
- Instructions for safely isolating the system?

I didn’t appreciate how useful this would be until somebody needed to assess what I actually had.

### 4. Check access and housekeeping

Are exits clear? Can you reach the isolation switch without moving equipment? Is the extinguisher accessible?

Are towels, bottles or loose equipment stored where they could fall into electrical equipment or block ventilation?

You don’t have to touch a wire to spot some of these problems.

### 5. Book an electrical inspection

Ask for an assessment of the whole high-current installation, not just whether one visible cable looks okay.

That includes cable sizing, terminations, routing, battery restraint, overcurrent protection, isolation and the manufacturer’s installation requirements.

A visual check by an owner cannot verify a hidden crimp. Mine is a fairly convincing example of that.

## About the $40 infrared thermometer

I bought an infrared thermometer at Canadian Tire for about $40.

I think it can be a useful thing to own, but I need to qualify my original “everyone should get one” reaction.

It measures surface temperature. It cannot see through heat-shrink, look inside a lug or certify that wiring is safe. Shiny metal can give misleading readings, and a small hot connection can be difficult to measure accurately.

**A cool reading does not clear an installation.**

I’m going to ask Priya which accessible surfaces, if any, are useful for me to monitor once the repaired system has been tested and cleared for use.

I am not switching a damaged system back on to get readings, and I’m not recommending that anyone else run a high-load test on wiring they already suspect is unsafe.

Think of it as a possible monitoring tool after professional guidance, not a substitute for an inspection.

## Tasha, please ask before paying that deposit

This is the part I especially want Tasha to read.

Before you pay a deposit to any van builder, ask for the electrical specifications **in writing**.

Not just “it’ll handle your dryer.”

Ask:

- What equipment can run at the same time?
- What battery voltage and inverter model are being supplied?
- What cable sizes and lengths are specified for the main runs?
- How were those sizes selected?
- What fuse types and ratings are being used, and where will they be installed?
- Who designs, installs and checks the electrical work?
- What standards and manufacturer instructions will the installation follow?
- Will you receive a diagram and test records?
- Can an independent electrician inspect it before final payment?

A builder doesn’t need to answer every technical question instantly. But they should be willing to provide clear documentation and explain who is responsible for the design.

I would also budget for an independent inspection before putting a new conversion to work.

Not because you should have to become an electrician to buy a grooming van. Because most of us are buying something we cannot properly assess ourselves.

## Where things stand with the builder

As I write this, Darren hasn’t answered three texts and an email.

I’m naming the business because it built my van and that is relevant to what happened. I’m not asking anyone to contact him, pile onto his pages or turn this into something uglier.

I can describe my installation, the damage and what Priya reported finding. I cannot speak for every van Coastline has built, and I don’t know why Darren hasn’t replied.

If he responds with information relevant to this account, I’ll update the post.

Right now, I’m keeping the photographs, messages and repair paperwork together.

## The bit that isn’t electrical

Moose’s mum brought me a coffee and sat with me on her front steps while I shook.

I keep remembering that.

Once Moose was out and the immediate panic had passed, I couldn’t stop shaking. Then, eventually, I started doing appointment maths.

I’ve cancelled **31 appointments so far**.

The repair quote is **$4,200** for rewiring the main runs, a new fuse block and a Class T fuse. Parts are on order. The estimate is at least **three weeks off the road**.

Insurance has said maybe. The adjuster is due Thursday. I don’t have a coverage decision yet.

Rent is due on the first.

I’m relieved, scared, angry and bored of hearing my own brain go through every possible version of what could have happened. Sometimes all of that arrives in the same ten minutes.

For now, the van is out of service while I wait for the repairs. I’m not putting a dog back in it until the electrical work has been repaired and checked.

If you take one thing from this, let it be that a neat-looking conversion is not proof of a safe electrical installation. Ask for the specifications. Keep the paperwork. Get someone qualified to look.

I’ll post another update when the van is back, with what was repaired and where things landed with insurance.

And Moose, if you’re reading this: sorry about the damp bum. Very glad we both got out.
